question: What shape is the earth and what is its diameter?
source_text: The earth, as everybody knows nowadays, is a spheroid, a sphere slightly compressed, orange fashion, with a diameter of nearly 8,000 miles.

question: By how much is the earth's axis shorter than its equatorial diameter?
source_text: We know now that it rotates upon its axis (which is about 24 miles shorter than its equatorial diameter) every twenty-four hours,

question: At what average distance does the moon circle the earth?
source_text: About the earth circles a smaller sphere, the moon, at an average distance of 239,000 miles.

question: What are the mean distances of Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune?
source_text: there are Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune at mean distances of 141, 483, 886, 1,782, and 1,793 millions of miles respectively.

question: If the earth were represented as a ball one inch in diameter, how big would the sun be and how far away?
source_text: If, then, we represent our earth as a little ball of one inch diameter, the sun would be a big globe nine feet across and 323 yards away, that is about a fifth of a mile, four or five minutes’ walking.

question: On the scale where the earth is one inch across, how far away would the nearest star be?
source_text: The nearest star to earth on this scale would be 40,000 miles away.

question: How far down into the earth and how far above its surface does life penetrate?
source_text: It does not penetrate much more than three miles down into the 4,000 miles that separate us from the centre of our globe, and it does not reach more than five miles above its surface.

question: How long is the earth estimated to have existed as a spinning planet flying round the sun?
source_text: It now seems probable that the earth has had an independent existence as a spinning planet flying round and round the sun for a longer period than 2,000,000,000 years.

question: What is the whole compass of time represented by the record of the rocks estimated to be?
source_text: The whole compass of time represented by the record of the rocks is now estimated as 1,600,000,000 years.

question: How long were the largest of the sea scorpions?
source_text: Among the largest were certain of the sea scorpions, which measured nine feet in length.

question: Which two characteristics does living matter possess that no dead matter possesses?
source_text: They can assimilate other matter into themselves and make it part of themselves, and they can reproduce themselves. They eat and they breed.

question: What kind of deduction is the process called Natural Selection?
source_text: This process, which is called Natural Selection, is not so much a scientific theory as a necessary deduction from the facts of reproduction and individual difference.

question: Where do nearly all authorities agree that life probably began?
source_text: But nearly all authorities are agreed that it probably began upon mud or sand in warm sunlit shallow brackish water, and that it spread up the beaches to the intertidal lines and out to the open waters.

question: What were the first shells and body armour of living things probably protections against?
source_text: Probably the first shells and body armour of living things were protections against drying rather than against active enemies.

question: How old do many geologists suppose the Silurian division to be, and which animals first appear in it?
source_text: which many geologists now suppose to be as old as five hundred million years, there appears a new type of being, equipped with eyes and teeth and swimming powers of an altogether more powerful kind. These were the first known backboned animals, the earliest fishes, the first known Vertebrata.

question: Which period of the Record of the Rocks has been called the Age of Fishes?
source_text: These fishes increase greatly in the next division of rocks, the rocks known as the Devonian system. They are so prevalent that this period of the Record of the Rocks has been called the Age of Fishes.

question: How long were the fishes of the Devonian system?
source_text: Few of them were more than two or three feet long, but there were exceptional forms which were as long as twenty feet.

question: How far did the wings of the dragon flies of the coal swamp period spread out?
source_text: There were dragon flies in this period with wings that spread out to twenty-nine inches.

question: Which organ of the fish becomes the lung in the vertebrated line?
source_text: The old gills with which the ancestral fish of the vertebrated line had breathed were inadaptable to breathing upon land, and in the case of this division of the animal kingdom it is the swimming bladder of the fish which becomes a new, deep-seated breathing organ, the lung.

question: Why was there no real soil during the Age of Fishes?
source_text: There was no real soil—for as yet there were no earthworms which help to make a soil, and no plants to break up the rock particles into mould; there was no trace of moss or lichen.

question: How long is the Mesozoic period supposed to have lasted?
source_text: The period lasted altogether, it is now supposed, upwards of two hundred million years.

question: Why is the Mesozoic period also called the Age of Reptiles, and when did it end?
source_text: and it is also called the Age of Reptiles because of the astonishing predominance and variety of this form of life. It came to an end some eighty million years ago.

question: How long were the Diplodocus Carnegii and the Gigantosaurus?
source_text: The _Diplodocus Carnegii_ for example measured eighty-four feet from snout to tail; the Gigantosaurus was even greater; it measured a hundred feet.

question: Which were the first flying creatures with backbones?
source_text: These were the Pterodactyls. These were the first flying creatures with backbones; they mark a new achievement in the growing powers of vertebrated life.

question: Which three groups of big swimming beings invaded the sea during the Mesozoic?
source_text: Three groups of big swimming beings had invaded the sea from which their ancestors had come: the Mososaurs, the Plesiosaurs, and Ichthyosaurs.

question: What kind of feathers does the New Zealand Ki-Wi have, and what came first in the development of birds?
source_text: That peculiarly primitive bird, the New Zealand Ki-Wi, has feathers of a very simple sort, and neither flies nor appears to be descended from flying ancestors. In the development of the birds, feathers came before wings.

question: Which two mammals still live that lay eggs and have no proper mammæ?
source_text: Two mammals still live which lay eggs and which have not proper mammæ, though they nourish their young by a nutritive secretion of the under skin; these are the duck-billed platypus and the echidna.

question: How does the echidna carry its eggs?
source_text: The echidna lays leathery eggs and then puts them into a pouch under its belly, and so carries them about warm and safe until they hatch.

question: How many years are estimated to have elapsed from the beginnings of the Cainozoic period to the present time?
source_text: It is estimated now that between forty and eighty million years have elapsed from the beginnings of the Cainozoic period to the present time.

question: Which plants appear with the opening of the Cainozoic period?
source_text: With the opening of this period the grasses appear; for the first time there is pasture in the world

question: How did the brain capacity of the Titanotherium compare with that of the modern rhinoceros?
source_text: There is a creature, the Titanotherium, which lived in the earliest division of this period. It was probably very like a modern rhinoceros in its habits and needs. But its brain capacity was not one tenth that of its living successor.

question: Which animals does the order Primates include?
source_text: At the head of these is the order _Primates_, which includes the lemurs, the monkeys, apes and man.

question: How long ago had primitive monkeys and lemuroid creatures appeared?
source_text: But we know that quite early in the Cainozoic period, that is to say some forty million years ago or so, primitive monkeys and lemuroid creatures had appeared, poorer in brain and not so specialized as their later successors.

question: How far south did the Arctic ice cap reach in England and in America during the great Ice Age?
source_text: In England it came almost down to the Thames, in America it reached Ohio.

question: When was the First Glacial Age coming on and when did the Fourth Glacial Age reach its bitterest?
source_text: The First Glacial Age was coming on 600,000 years ago; the Fourth Glacial Age reached its bitterest some fifty thousand years ago.

question: What are “Eoliths”?
source_text: we find flints and stones that have evidently been chipped intentionally by some handy creature desirous of hammering, scraping or fighting with the sharpened edge. These things have been called “Eoliths” (dawn stones).

question: What is the creature called whose skull fragment and bones were found at Trinil in Java?
source_text: This creature is now called _Pithecanthropus erectus_, the walking ape man, and the little trayful of its bones is the only help our imaginations have as yet in figuring to, ourselves the makers of the Eoliths.

question: What was found in a sandpit at Heidelberg and why is articulate speech thought improbable for it?
source_text: Then, in a sandpit at Heidelberg, appears a single quasi-human jaw-bone, a clumsy jaw-bone, absolutely chinless, far heavier than a true human jaw-bone and narrower, so that it is improbable the creature’s tongue could have moved about for articulate speech.

question: What have scientific men named the creature found at Piltdown?
source_text: Scientific men have named him Eoanthropus, the Dawn Man. He stands apart from his kindred; a very different being either from the Heidelberg creature or from any living ape.

question: What was unusual about the thumbs and necks of the Neanderthalers?
source_text: Their thumbs were not opposable to the fingers as men’s are; their necks were so poised that they could not turn back their heads and look up to the sky.

question: What was found at Broken Hill in South Africa in the summer of 1921?
source_text: But in the summer of 1921, an extremely interesting skull was found together with pieces of a skeleton at Broken Hill in South Africa, which seems to be a relic of a third sort of man, intermediate in its characteristics between the Neanderthaler and the human being.

question: Where have the earliest traces of a humanity indisputably kindred with ourselves been found, and how old are they?
source_text: Bones, weapons, scratchings upon bone and rock, carved fragments of bone, and paintings in caves and upon rock surfaces dating. it is supposed. from 30,000 years ago or more, have been discovered in both these countries.

question: Which country is at present the richest in the world in the first relics of our real human ancestors?
source_text: Spain is at present the richest country in the world in these first relics of our real human ancestors.

question: Why does the author not mention America when discussing where earlier human remains might be found?
source_text: I write in Asia or Africa, and I do not mention America because so far there have been no finds at all of any of the higher Primates, either of great apes, sub-men, Neanderthalers nor early true men.

question: After which cave are the Cro-Magnards named?
source_text: From the Cro-Magnon cave in which the first skeletons were found these people have been called Cro-Magnards. They were savages, but savages of a high order.

question: Which weapons did the earliest true men hunt with, and which animals had they not tamed?
source_text: They hunted with spears and throwing stones. They do not seem to have had the bow, and it is doubtful if they had yet learnt to tame any animals. They had no dogs.

question: Who were the Azilians and after which cave are they named?
source_text: These were the Azilians (named from the Mas d’Azil cave). They had the bow; they seem to have worn feather headdresses; they drew vividly;

question: Which new age was beginning when men learnt to polish and grind stone implements?
source_text: By ten or twelve thousand years a new sort of life has dawned in Europe, men have learnt not only to chip but to polish and grind stone implements, and they have begun cultivation. The Neolithic Age (New Stone Age) was beginning.

question: Which anthropological writer wrote Primal Law and what did he explain in it?
source_text: An anthropological writer of great genius, J. J. Atkinson, in his _Primal Law_, has shown how much of the customary law of savages, the _Tabus_, that are so remarkable a fact in tribal life,

question: How recent a development is systematic thinking in human experience?
source_text: Systematic thinking is apparently a comparatively late development in human experience; it has not played any great part in human life until within the last three thousand years.

question: Who was the first priest in primitive society?
source_text: The expert in Fetish, the Medicine Man, was the first priest. He exhorted, he interpreted dreams, he warned, he performed the complicated hocus pocus that brought luck or averted calamity.

question: What did man learn to do with wild wheat before he learnt to sow?
source_text: Somewhere in the Mediterranean region, wheat grew wild; and man may have learnt to pound and then grind up its seeds for food long before he learnt to sow. He reaped before he sowed.

question: In which monumental work is the association of sowing with blood sacrifice fully developed?
source_text: the interested reader will find it very fully developed in that monumental work, Sir J. G. Frazer’s _Golden Bough_.

question: What was the first chronology reckoned in?
source_text: The first chronology was in lunar months; it is supposed that the years of the Biblical patriarchs are really moons, and the Babylonian calendar shows distinct traces of an attempt to reckon seed time by taking thirteen lunar months to see it round.

question: Who used the term “Heliolithic culture” and what does the word mean?
source_text: Eliot Smith and Rivers have used the term “Heliolithic culture” for the culture of these first agricultural peoples. “Heliolithic” (Sun and Stone)

question: What was the old custom known as the couvade?
source_text: they had the old custom, known as the _couvade_, of sending the _father_ to bed and rest when a child was born, and they had as a luck symbol the well-known Swastika.

question: What had happened to the barrier across the Straits of Gibraltar by about 10,000 B.C.?
source_text: It is probable that by that time the great barrier across the Straits of Gibraltar that had hitherto banked back the ocean waters from the Mediterranean valley had been eaten through, and that the Mediterranean was a sea following much the same coastlines as it does now.

question: Which large animals did the first people to reach America find there?
source_text: They found caribou, the American reindeer, in the north and great herds of bison the Glyptodon, a gigantic armadillo, and the Megatherium, a monstrous clumsy sloth as high as an elephant.

question: In which regions of America did civilizations arise about 1000 B.C.?
source_text: But in Mexico, Yucatan and Peru conditions existed favourable to settled cultivation, and here about 1000 B.C. or so arose very interesting civilizations of a parallel but different type from the old-world civilization.

question: Which metals did the American tribes chiefly possess, and which did they never discover?
source_text: They never discovered the use of iron, and their chief metal possessions were native gold and copper.

question: By which method were records kept in Peru instead of writing?
source_text: In Peru there were beginnings of a similar writing but they were superseded by a method of keeping records by knotting cords.

question: Where did the Sumerians build their first cities?
source_text: In those days the Euphrates and Tigris flowed by separate mouths into the Persian Gulf, and it was in the country between them that the Sumerians built their first cities.

question: Which animals did the Sumerians have and how did they fight?
source_text: They had cattle, sheep, goats and asses, but no horses. They fought on foot, in close formation, carrying spears and shields of skin.

question: Which is the first recorded empire and where is it recorded?
source_text: A very ancient inscription at Nippur records the “empire,” the first recorded empire, of the Sumerian city of Erech.

question: Why is Sumerian writing called cuneiform?
source_text: From the fact that the wooden styles used in Sumeria made wedge-shaped marks, the Sumerian writing is called cuneiform (= wedge-shaped).

question: From which two scripts did all the true alphabets of the later world derive?
source_text: All the true alphabets of the later world derived from a mixture of the Sumerian cuneiform and the Egyptian hieroglyphic (priest writing).

question: Who was raised above the priests in Egypt?
source_text: In Egypt however there was one who was raised above the priests; he was the living incarnation of the chief god of the land, the Pharaoh, the god king.

question: How high is the largest of the pyramids at Gizeh and what is the weight of stone in it?
source_text: The largest of these is 450 feet high and the weight of stone in it is 4,883,000 tons.

question: Which people were founding cities on the upper Tigris?
source_text: On the upper Tigris a people called the Assyrians were founding cities; in the valleys of Asia Minor and on the Mediterranean shores and islands, there were small communities growing up to civilization.

question: When was the domestic fowl domesticated by man?
source_text: (But hens they would not steal, because the domestic fowl—an Indian jungle fowl originally was not domesticated by man until about 1000 B.C.)

question: What did Sargon conquer about 2750 B.C. and how far did his mastery extend?
source_text: About 2750 B.C. a great Semitic leader, Sargon, had conquered the whole Sumerian land and was master of all the world from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean Sea.

question: Which king consolidated the first Babylonian Empire and what did he make?
source_text: It was consolidated by a great king called Hammurabi (circa 2100 B.C.) who made the earliest code of laws yet known to history.

question: When were the Semitic conquerors of Egypt expelled and how were they regarded there?
source_text: These Semitic conquerors never assimilated themselves with the Egyptians; they were always regarded with hostility as foreigners and barbarians; and they were at last expelled by a popular uprising about 1600 B.C.

question: By when were there ships on the Mediterranean and Persian Gulf?
source_text: There were ships upon the Red Sea long before the pyramids were built, and there were ships on the Mediterranean and Persian Gulf by 7000 B.C.

question: When was Cretan civilization at its zenith and how far back does the history of Cnossos go?
source_text: The history of Cnossos goes back as far as the history of Egypt; the two countries were trading actively across the sea by 4000 B.C. By 2500 B.C., that is between the time of Sargon I and Hammurabi, Cretan civilization was at its zenith.

question: What was the Cretan monarch called and what conveniences did his palace have?
source_text: The monarch was called Minos, as the Egyptian monarch was called Pharaoh; and he kept his state in a palace fitted with running water, with bathrooms and the like conveniences such as we know of in no other ancient remains.

question: Which skilful Cretan artificer did the Greeks tell legends about?
source_text: because later on the Greeks told legends of a certain skilful Cretan artificer, Dædalus, who attempted to make some sort of flying machine, perhaps a glider, which collapsed and fell into the sea.

question: When was the palace of Minos destroyed?
source_text: But about 1400 B.C. disaster came perhaps very suddenly upon its prosperity. The palace of Minos was destroyed, and its ruins have never been rebuilt or inhabited from that day to this.

question: Who conquered Babylon in 745 B.C. and what did he found?
source_text: Tiglath Pileser III conquered Babylon in 745 B.C. and founded what historians call the New Assyrian Empire.

question: Which people are said to have become known in history as the Philistines?
source_text: some built themselves cities upon the south- east coasts of the Mediterranean and became later that people known in history as the Philistines.

question: Which literature did the Hebrews produce that became of great importance in subsequent history?
source_text: They produced a literature of very great importance in subsequent history, a collection of books, histories, poems, books of wisdom and prophetic works, the Hebrew Bible.

question: Which beast of burthen was used in Babylon and Egypt, and which animal had not been brought into Egypt?
source_text: The beast of burthen was the ass; the horse was still used only in chariots for war and upon occasions of state. The mule was still novel and the camel, though it was known in Mesopotamia, had not been brought into Egypt.

question: How was gold and silver kept for exchange in Babylon before coinage?
source_text: Gold and silver were used for exchange and kept in ingots; and there were bankers, before coinage, who stamped their names and the weight on these lumps of precious metal.

question: Which two articles of diet were absent from the crowning cities of the ancient world?
source_text: A modern visitor to these crowning cities of the ancient world would have missed two very important articles of diet; there were no hens and no eggs.

question: Which Chinese dynasty was contemporary with the seventeenth dynasty in Egypt?
source_text: Contemporary with the seventeenth dynasty in Egypt, there was a dynasty of emperors in China, the Shang dynasty, priest emperors over a loose-knit empire of subordinate kings.

question: What are the “round barrows” that occur all over north Europe?
source_text: They put the ashes of their greater leaders in urns and then made a great circular mound about them. These mounds are the “round barrows” that occur all over north Europe.

question: Which people reached Britain and Ireland armed with bronze weapons?
source_text: The first of these people who reached Britain and Ireland were armed with bronze weapons. They exterminated or subjugated the people who had made the great stone monuments of Carnac in Brittany and Stonehenge and Avebury in England. They reached Ireland. They are called the Goidelic Celts.

question: When does Rome first appear in history and who ruled it then?
source_text: In the eighth century B.C. Rome appears in history, a trading town on the Tiber, inhabited by Aryan Latins but under the rule of Etruscan nobles and kings.

question: Why did the Assyrian usurper adopt the name Sargon?
source_text: Sargon was not this man’s original name; he adopted it to flatter the conquered Babylonians by reminding them of that ancient founder of the Akkadian Empire, Sargon I, two thousand years before his time.

question: Which peoples combined against Nineveh and in which year was the city taken?
source_text: A Semitic people from south-east Mesopotamia, the Chaldeans, combined with Aryan Medes and Persians from the north-east against Nineveh, and in 606 B.C.—for now we are coming down to exact chronology—took that city.

question: Whom did Necho II defeat and slay at the battle of Megiddo in 608 B.C.?
source_text: He had defeated and slain King Josiah of Judah, a small country of which there is more to tell presently, at the battle of Megiddo in 608 B.C.,

question: What kind of library did Sardanapalus make?
source_text: He made a library, a library not of paper but of the clay tablets that were used for writing in Mesopotamia since early Sumerian days.

question: How did Cyrus take Babylon?
source_text: He came up against Babylon, there was a battle outside the walls, and the gates of the city were opened to him (538 B.C.). His soldiers entered the city without fighting.

question: Which territories did the Persian Empire of Darius I include?
source_text: It included all Asia Minor and Syria, all the old Assyrian and Babylonian empires, Egypt, the Caucasus and Caspian regions, Media, Persia, and it extended into India as far as the Indus.

question: Which were the great cities of the Persian empire and which was the capital?
source_text: Babylon though still important was now a declining city, and the great cities of the new empire were Persepolis and Susa and Ecbatana. The capital was Susa.

question: Of what did the Jewish Bible consist at the time of the return from Babylon?
source_text: Their Bible at that time seems to have consisted only of the Pentateuch, that is to say the first five books of the Old Testament as we know it.

question: How did Saul die and what happened to his body?
source_text: he perished under the hail of Philistine arrows at the battle of Mount Gilboa, his armour went into the temple of the Philistine Venus, and his body was nailed to the walls of Beth-shan.

question: How large would Solomon’s temple be if one works out the measurements?
source_text: Solomon’s temple, if one works out the measurements, would go inside a small suburban church, and his fourteen hundred chariots cease to impress us when we learn from an Assyrian monument that his successor Ahab sent a contingent of two thousand to the Assyrian army.

question: When was the kingdom of Israel swept away into captivity and by whom?
source_text: In 721 B.C. the kingdom of Israel was swept away into captivity by the Assyrians and its people utterly lost to history.

question: Which expedition sailed completely round Africa in the time of the Pharaoh Necho?
source_text: In the time of the Pharaoh Necho, a Phœnician expedition sailed completely round Africa.

question: What was foremost among the Jewish ideas about their God?
source_text: Foremost of these Jewish ideas was this, that their God was invisible and remote, an invisible God in a temple not made with hands, a Lord of Righteousness throughout the earth.

question: What were the origins of the Prophets Ezekiel and Amos?
source_text: The Prophet Ezekiel was of the priestly caste and the Prophet Amos wore the goatskin mantle of a shepherd, but all had this in common, that they gave allegiance to no one but to the God of Righteousness and that they spoke directly to the people.

question: What does the prophetic voice foreshadow in the great utterances of Isaiah?
source_text: In the great utterances of Isaiah the prophetic voice rises to a pitch of splendid anticipation and foreshadows the whole earth united and at peace under one God. Therein the Jewish prophecies culminate.

question: Which animals lived in Mesopotamia and Greece in the days of Thothmes?
source_text: For in those days there were elephants in Mesopotamia and lions in Greece.

question: What do the two great Greek epics, the Iliad and the Odyssey, tell of?
source_text: two great epics, the _Iliad_, telling how a league of Greek tribes besieged and took and sacked the town of Troy in Asia Minor, and the _Odyssey_, being a long adventure story of the return of the sage captain, Odysseus, from Troy to his own island.

question: In the cities of the Greeks, did the wall or the temple come first?
source_text: It has been said that the cities of the primitive civilizations grew up about the altar of some tribal god, and that the wall was added; in the cities of the Greeks the wall preceded the temple.

question: How large were the Greek states and their cities?
source_text: The largest states were smaller than many English counties, and it is doubtful if the population of any of their cities ever exceeded a third of a million. Few came up even to 50,000.

question: Which two things held all Greece together in a certain community of feeling?
source_text: Yet all Greece was held together in a certain community of feeling by two things, by the epics and by the custom of taking part every fourth year in the athletic contests at Olympia.

question: How did the Greek democracies differ from modern democracies?
source_text: The Greek democracies were not like our modern “democracies” in which everyone has a vote. Many of the Greek democracies had a few hundred or a few thousand citizens and then many thousands of slaves, freedmen and so forth, with no share in public affairs.

question: Who was teaching in India and in China during the sixth century B.C.?
source_text: but as we shall tell later Gautama Buddha was then teaching in India and Confucius and Lao Tse in China. From Athens to the Pacific the human mind was astir.

question: Why did Darius I invade Europe?
source_text: It was on account of the Scythians that Darius I invaded Europe. He wanted to reach South Russia, the homeland of the Scythian horsemen.

question: How far and how fast did the runner sent from Athens to Sparta travel?
source_text: This runner (the prototype of all “Marathon” runners) did over a hundred miles of broken country in less than two days.

question: How large was the force under Leonidas at the pass of Thermopylæ?
source_text: At the narrow pass of Thermopylæ a small force of 1400 men under the Spartan Leonidas resisted this multitude, and after a fight of unsurpassed heroism was completely destroyed.

question: Where and when was Herodotus born, and which countries did he visit?
source_text: This Herodotus was born about 484 B.C. in the Ionian city of Halicarnassus in Asia Minor, and he visited Babylon and Egypt in his search for exact particulars.

question: For how long was Athens dominated by Pericles and what did he set himself to do?
source_text: For over thirty years (466 to 428 B.C.) Athens was dominated by a man of great vigour and liberality of mind, Pericles, who set himself to rebuild the city from the ashes to which the Persians had reduced it.

question: When was Socrates executed and in what manner was he condemned to die?
source_text: In the end Socrates was executed for disturbing people’s minds (399 B.C.), he was condemned after the dignified fashion of the Athens of those days to drink in his own house and among his own friends a poisonous draught made from hemlock,

question: Who was the first man to write a Utopia and what is a Utopia?
source_text: He was the first man to write a Utopia, that is to say the plan of a community different from and better than any existing community.

question: How many different states’ constitutions did Aristotle’s students at the Lyceum examine and compare?
source_text: His students at the Lyceum examined and compared the constitutions of 158 different states

question: What military innovations did Philip introduce in his infantry and his mounted gentlemen?
source_text: Philip made his infantry fight in a closely packed mass, the Macedonian phalanx, and he trained his mounted gentlemen, the knights or companions, to fight in formation and so invented cavalry.

question: Whom did Alexander defeat at Issus in 333 B.C.?
source_text: At Issus (333 B.C.) he met and smashed a vast conglomerate host under Darius III.

question: Where did Alexander meet Darius and fight the decisive battle of the war?
source_text: At Arbela near the ruins of Nineveh, which was already a forgotten city, he met Darius and fought the decisive battle of the war.

question: Which Indian king did Alexander fight on the Indus, and what did his troops meet there for the first time?
source_text: He fought a great battle on the Indus with an Indian king, Porus, and here the Macedonian troops met elephants for the first time and defeated them.

question: Which parts of Alexander’s empire did Seleucus, Ptolemy and Antigonus take?
source_text: One of his generals, Seleucus, retained most of the old Persian empire from the Indus to Ephesus; another, Ptolemy, seized Egypt, and Antigonus secured Macedonia.

question: Who led the ten thousand Greek mercenaries and in which work is their return described?
source_text: a band of ten thousand Greek mercenaries played a part under the leadership of Xenophon. Their return to Asiatic Greece from Babylon is described in his _Retreat of the Ten Thousand_,

question: Who was the first person to make a permanent endowment of science, and what did he set up?
source_text: Alexander had already devoted considerable sums to finance the enquiries of Aristotle, but Ptolemy I was the first person to make a permanent endowment of science. He set up a foundation in Alexandria which was formerly dedicated to the Muses, the Museum of Alexandria.

question: Who was Herophilus and what is he said to have practised?
source_text: Herophilus was one of the greatest of Greek anatomists, and is said to have practised vivisection.

question: Where was paper invented and when did it reach the western world?
source_text: Paper was a Chinese invention and it did not reach the western world until the ninth century A.D.

question: Who were the Parthians and how did they treat the Græco-Persian empire?
source_text: These were the Parthians, hosts of mounted bowmen, who treated the Græco-Persian empire of Persepolis and Susa in the third century B.C. in much the same fashion that the Medes and Persians had treated it in the seventh and sixth.

question: When did an Aryan-speaking people come down into India, and what was their variety of Aryan speech called?
source_text: Somewhen perhaps about 2000 B.C., an Aryan- speaking people came down from the north-west into India either in one invasion or in a series of invasions; and was able to spread its language and traditions over most of north India. Its peculiar variety of Aryan speech was the Sanskrit.

question: What was Siddhattha Gautama’s family background and at what age was he married?
source_text: Siddhattha Gautama was the son of an aristocratic family which ruled a small district on the Himalayan slopes. He was married at nineteen to a beautiful cousin.

question: What happened in the night after the feast celebrating the birth of Gautama’s son?
source_text: There was a great feast and a Nautch dance to celebrate the birth of this new tie, and in the night Gautama awoke in a great agony of spirit, “like a man who is told that his house is on fire.

question: What did Gautama do beside the sandy river after riding away from his clan?
source_text: There he cut off his flowing locks with his sword, removed all his ornaments and sent them and his horse and sword back to his house.

question: What had Gautama realized when he refused to continue his mortifications?
source_text: He had realized that whatever truth a man may reach is reached best by a nourished brain in a healthy body.

question: What is attained when self has vanished altogether, according to Gautama’s teaching?
source_text: When they were overcome, when self had vanished altogether, then serenity of soul, Nirvana, the highest good was attained.

question: What did Chandragupta achieve in 303 B.C.?
source_text: He built up an empire in North India and was presently (303 B.C.) able to attack Seleucus I in the Punjab and drive the last vestige of Greek power out of India.

question: Which country did Asoka invade in 255 B.C. and how did he react to his own success?
source_text: He invaded Kalinga (255 B.C.), a country on the east coast of Madras, he was successful in his military operations and—alone among conquerors—he was so disgusted by the cruelty and horror of war that he renounced it.

question: To which places did missionaries go from Asoka?
source_text: Missionaries went from Asoka to Kashmir, to Persia, to Ceylon and Alexandria.

question: When did the Shang dynasty come to an end and which dynasty succeeded it?
source_text: The “Shang” dynasty came to an end in 1125 B.C. A “Chow” dynasty succeeded “Shang,” and maintained China in a relaxing unity until the days of Asoka in India and of the Ptolemies in Egypt.

question: How many practically independent states were there in China in the sixth century B.C.?
source_text: There was in the sixth century B.C., says one Chinese authority, five or six thousand practically independent states in China. It was what the Chinese call in their records an “Age of Confusion.”

question: What was Confucius’s origin and what did he set up in the state of Lu?
source_text: Confucius was a man of aristocratic origin and some official importance in a small state called Lu. Here in a very parallel mood to the Greek impulse he set up a sort of Academy for discovering and teaching Wisdom.

question: What position did Lao Tse hold for a long time?
source_text: The teaching of Lao Tse, who was for a long time in charge of the imperial library of the Chow dynasty, was much more mystical and vague and elusive than that of Confucius.

question: Who was called “the First Universal Emperor” in the Chinese Chronicles?
source_text: His son, Shi-Hwang-ti (king in 246 B.C., emperor in 220 B.C.), is called in the Chinese Chronicles “the First Universal Emperor.”

question: Why did Shi-Hwang-ti begin the Great Wall of China?
source_text: He fought vigorously against the Hunnish invaders from the northern deserts, and he began that immense work, the Great Wall of China, to set a limit to their incursions.

question: Which date did the old chronologies give for the founding of Rome?
source_text: The old chronologies gave 753 B.C. as the date of the founding of Rome, half a century later than the founding of the great Phœnician city of Carthage and twenty-three years after the first Olympiad.

question: When were the Etruscan kings expelled and what did Rome become?
source_text: In that red-letter century, the sixth century B.C., the Etruscan kings were expelled (510 B.C.) and Rome became an aristocratic republic with a lordly class of “patrician” families dominating a commonalty of “plebeians.”

question: How was the Gauls’ attempted night surprise on the Capitol betrayed?
source_text: An attempted night surprise was betrayed by the cackling of some geese, and finally the invaders were bought off and retired to the north of Italy again.

question: Why did Pyrrhus abandon his dream of conquest and go home?
source_text: Repulsed by the Romans, endangered at sea by the Carthaginians, and threatened at home by the Gauls, Pyrrhus abandoned his dream of conquest and went home (275 B.C.), and the power of Rome was extended to the Straits of Messina.

question: How did the Carthaginian quinqueremes compare with the battleships at Salamis?
source_text: They had great fighting ships of what was hitherto an unheard-of size, quinqueremes, galleys with five banks of oars and a huge ram. At the battle of Salamis, two centuries before, the leading battleships had only been triremes with three banks.

question: With whom did the Romans man their new navy and what did they invent?
source_text: They manned the new navy they created chiefly with Greek seamen, and they invented grappling and boarding to make up for the superior seamanship of the enemy.

question: At which battle were the last naval forces of Carthage defeated?
source_text: The last naval forces of Carthage were defeated by it last Roman effort at the battle of the Ægatian Isles (241 B.C.) and Carthage sued for peace.

question: Who led the Carthaginians across the Ebro in 218 B.C.?
source_text: At last in 218 B.C. the Carthaginians, provoked by new Roman aggressions, did cross this river under a young general named Hannibal, one of the most brilliant commanders in the whole of history.

question: At which battles did Hannibal inflict tremendous defeats upon the Romans?
source_text: He inflicted tremendous defeats upon the Romans at Lake Trasimere and at Cannæ, and throughout all his Italian campaigns no Roman army stood against him and escaped disaster.

question: Where and at whose hands did Hannibal experience his first defeat?
source_text: a Roman army crossed into Africa, and Hannibal experienced his first defeat under its walls at the battle of Zama (202 B.C. at the hands of Scipio Africanus the Elder.

question: How long did the street fighting last when Carthage was stormed, and how many citizens remained alive?
source_text: The street fighting, or massacre, lasted six days; it was extraordinarily bloody, and when the citadel capitulated only about fifty thousand of the Carthaginian population remained alive out of a quarter of a million.

question: When was Jerusalem taken by the Romans and when was it besieged and captured?
source_text: Jerusalem, which has always been rather the symbol than the centre of Judaism, was taken by the Romans in 65 B.C.; and after various vicissitudes of quasi- independence and revolt was besieged by them in 70 A.D. and captured after a stubborn struggle.

question: When did all the free inhabitants of Italy become citizens of the city of Rome?
source_text: In 89 B.C. all the free inhabitants of Italy became citizens of the city of Rome.

question: What is the first stage of Roman expansion called and when did it begin?
source_text: The first stage began after the sack of Rome by the Goths in 390 B.C. and went on until the end of the First Punic War (240 B.C,). We may call this stage the stage of the Assimilative Republic.

question: How was Sicily treated after the First Punic War?
source_text: Sicily for instance was treated as a conquered prey. It was declared an “estate” of the Roman people. Its rich soil and industrious population was exploited to make Rome rich.

question: Was any form of representative government introduced into the Roman republic?
source_text: Nothing of the nature of representative government was ever introduced into the Roman republic. No one thought of electing delegates to represent the will of the citizens.

question: Where did Spartacus hold out for two years?
source_text: For two years Spartacus held out in the crater of Vesuvius, which seemed at that time to be an extinct volcano.

question: Which phase in the development of Roman power began with Marius?
source_text: With Marius began the third phase in the development of the Roman power, the Republic of the Military Commanders. For now began a period in which the leaders of the paid legions fought for the mastery of the Roman world.

question: When was Pompey defeated by Julius Cæsar and where was he murdered?
source_text: After a long rivalry Pompey was defeated by Julius Cæsar (48 B.C.) and murdered in Egypt, leaving Julius Cæsar sole master of the Roman world.

question: Which river marked the boundary between Cæsar’s command and Italy, and when did he cross it?
source_text: It was illegal for a general to bring his troops out of the boundary of his command, and the boundary between Cæsar’s command and Italy was the Rubicon. In 49 B.C. he crossed the Rubicon, saying “The die is cast” and marched upon Pompey and Rome.

question: What inscription was placed on Cæsar’s statue in the temple?
source_text: His statue was set up in a temple with an inscription “To the Unconquerable God.”

question: By which titles was Octavian to be called and during which years did he reign?
source_text: He was to be called not King indeed, but “Princeps” and “Augustus.” He became Augustus Cæsar, the first of the Roman emperors (27 B.C. to 14 A.D.).

question: Which walls did Hadrian build against the northern barbarians?
source_text: Like Shi-Hwang-ti he built walls against the northern barbarians; one across Britain and a palisade between the Rhine and the Danube.

question: Which Chinese expeditionary force reached the Caspian in 102 A.D.?
source_text: In 102 A.D. a Chinese expeditionary force under Pan Chau reached the Caspian, and sent emissaries to report upon the power of Rome.

question: How did China at this time compare with the Roman Empire?
source_text: China at this time was the greatest, best organized and most civilized political system in the world. It was superior in area and population to the Roman Empire at its zenith.

question: Who afflicted India for a large part of the fifth century A.D.?
source_text: For a large part of the fifth century A.D. India was afflicted by the Ephthalites or White Huns, who levied tribute on the small Indian princes and held India in terror.

question: Which emperor did the Goths defeat and kill after crossing the Danube in 247?
source_text: In 247 they crossed the Danube in a great land raid, and defeated and killed the Emperor Decius in a battle in what is now Serbia.

question: In which parts of the empire did the Latin language never prevail, and which language did Saul of Tarsus write in?
source_text: Over Greece, Asia Minor, Egypt and the Hellenized East generally, the Latin language never prevailed. Greek ruled there invincibly. Saul of Tarsus, who became the apostle Paul, was a Jew and a Roman citizen; but he spoke and wrote Greek and not Hebrew.

question: Which language was the mother speech of Septimius Severus?
source_text: Septimius Severus, who was emperor from 193 to 211 A.D., spoke Carthaginian as his mother speech. He learnt Latin later as a foreign tongue; and it is recorded that his sister never learnt Latin and conducted her Roman household in the Punic language.

question: Which modern languages remain to remind us of the extension of Latin speech and customs?
source_text: The Roumanian, Italian, French and Spanish languages, all variations and modifications of Latin, remain to remind us of this extension of Latin speech and customs.

question: How was agricultural work done in Sparta and what was the special slave class called?
source_text: The Greek world had had very various methods of cultivation, from the Arcadian plan, wherein every free citizen toiled with his own hands, to Sparta, wherein it was a dishonour to work and where agricultural work was done by a special slave class, the Helots.

question: What happened to all the slaves of a household if a slave slew his master?
source_text: If a slave slew his master, all the slaves in his household and not merely the murderer were crucified.

question: Who was usually the tutor of a young Roman of good family?
source_text: The tutor of a young Roman of good family was usually a slave. A rich man would have a Greek slave as librarian, and slave secretaries and learned men.

question: How did the intellectual output of the Roman empire compare with that of Athens?
source_text: but the whole Roman empire in four centuries produced nothing to set beside the bold and noble intellectual activities of the comparatively little city of Athens during its one century of greatness.

question: What is theocrasia?
source_text: This fusion of gods is called theocrasia; and the age of the great conquests of the thousand years B.C. was an age of theocrasia.

question: Who was Isis identified with, and who was her child?
source_text: Isis was also Hathor, a cow-goddess, and the crescent moon and the Star of the sea. Osiris dies and she bears a child, Horus, who is also a hawk-god and the dawn, and who grows to become Osiris again.

question: Which darker Egyptian gods lay beneath the triple group of Osiris, Isis and Horus?
source_text: Beneath this triple group there are other and darker Egyptian gods, bad gods, the dog-headed Anubis, black night and the like, devourers, tempters, enemies of god and man.

question: Which temple did Ptolemy I set up in Alexandria and which gods were worshipped there?
source_text: A great temple, the Serapeum, was set up by Ptolemy I at which a sort of trinity of gods was worshipped. These were Serapis (who was Osiris-Apis rechristened), Isis and Horus.

question: What was Serapis called and why was the idea of immortality eagerly received?
source_text: The idea of immortality, an immortality of compensations and consolation, was eagerly received by a world in which the common life was hopelessly wretched. Serapis was called “the saviour of souls.”

question: How did the images of Isis stand in her temples and who waited on her altar?
source_text: Her images stood in her temples, as Queen of Heaven, bearing the infant Horus in her arms. Candles were burnt before her, votive offerings were made to her, shaven priests consecrated to celibacy waited on her altar.

question: What was the origin of Mithraism and what did it centre upon?
source_text: This was a religion of Persian origin, and it centred upon some now forgotten mysteries about Mithras sacrificing a sacred and benevolent bull.

question: What happened to the votary of Mithraism at his initiation?
source_text: The votary to Mithraism actually bathed in the blood of the sacrificial bull. At his initiation he went beneath a scaffolding upon which a bull was killed so that the blood could actually run down on him.

question: Why would the Jews refuse to take part in the public sacrifices to Cæsar?
source_text: They held that their God was a jealous God intolerant of idolatry, and they would refuse to take part in the public sacrifices to Cæsar. They would not even salute the Roman standards for fear of idolatry.

question: Which Jewish sect abandoned the world for austerities and mystical contemplation?
source_text: Communities of men abandoned the world and gave themselves to austerities and mystical contemplation. Such was the sect of the Essenes.

question: What are the only direct sources of information about the life and teaching of Jesus?
source_text: Our only direct sources of information about the life and teaching of Jesus are the four Gospels. All four agree in giving us a picture of a very definite personality.

question: For how long did Jesus go about the country spreading his doctrine, and with whom was he crucified?
source_text: He went about the country for three years spreading his doctrine and then he came to Jerusalem and was accused of trying to set up a strange kingdom in Judea; he was tried upon this charge, and crucified together with two thieves.

question: Upon what did Jesus cast scorn in the parable of the Good Samaritan?
source_text: In the parable of the Good Samaritan Jesus cast scorn upon that natural tendency we all obey, to glorify our own people and to minimize the righteousness of other creeds and other races.

question: What was St. Paul’s original name and what was he conspicuous for at first?
source_text: Paul’s name was originally Saul, and he was conspicuous at first as an active persecutor of the little band of disciples after the crucifixion. Then he was suddenly converted to Christianity, and he changed his name to Paul.

question: Why was Christianity regarded with more suspicion than its rival religions?
source_text: But Christianity was regarded with more suspicion than its rivals because, like the Jews, its adherents would not perform acts of worship to the God Cæsar. This made it a seditious religion,

question: What did the Arians and the Sabellians teach about Jesus?
source_text: The Arians taught that Jesus was divine, but distant from and inferior to the Father. The Sabellians taught that Jesus was merely an aspect of the Father,

question: Which formula became the accepted formula of all Christendom and where is it most completely expressed?
source_text: For a time it seemed that Arianism would prevail over its rivals, and then after disputes, violence and wars, the Trinitarian formula became the accepted formula of all Christendom. It may be found in its completest expression in the Athanasian Creed.

question: What happened during the great persecution under the Emperor Diocletian?
source_text: The considerable accumulations of Church property were seized, all bibles and religious writings were confiscated and destroyed, Christians were put out of the protection of the law and many executed.

question: Why did the continued existence of the “book religions” depend on people being able to read?
source_text: These “book religions,” Christianity and Judaism, were religions that educated. Their continued existence depended very largely on people being able to read and understand their doctrinal ideas.

question: Who issued an edict of toleration in 317 and who became sole ruler of the Roman world in 324?
source_text: In 317 an edict of toleration was issued by the associated Emperor Galerius, and in 324 Constantine the Great, a friend and on his deathbed a baptized convert to Christianity, became sole ruler of the Roman world.

question: Where did Constantine decide to create a new permanent capital?
source_text: he decided to create a new permanent capital at Byzantium upon the Hellespont. This new-made Byzantium, which was re-christened Constantinople in his honour, was still building when he died.

question: When did Alaric take Rome?
source_text: In the course of their struggle Alaric marched into Italy and after a short siege took Rome (410 A.D.).

question: Which peoples submerged the Roman province of Britain and what became of their dialects?
source_text: but the Jutes, the Angles and Saxons who submerged the Roman province of Britain were agriculturalists and had no use for towns, they seem to have swept south Britain clear of the Romanized population and they replaced the language by their own Teutonic dialects, which became at last English.

question: Under which leader did the Vandals sail for North Africa and which city did they capture?
source_text: From Spain the Vandals under Genseric sailed for North Africa (429), captured Carthage (439), and built a fleet.

question: When did the Vandals capture and pillage Rome?
source_text: They secured the mastery of the sea and captured and pillaged Rome (455), which had recovered very imperfectly from her capture and looting by Alaric half a century earlier.

question: When did the Hun reach the eastern boundaries of European Russia and which century was the Hun’s century?
source_text: The Hun had reached the eastern boundaries of European Russia by the first century A.D., but it was not until the fourth and fifth centuries A.D. that these horsemen rose to predominance upon the steppes. The fifth century was the Hun’s century.

question: How far did Attila’s empire extend and with whom did he exchange ambassadors?
source_text: his empire extended from the Rhine cross the plains into Central Asia. He exchanged ambassadors with China. His head camp was in the plain of Hungary east of the Danube.

question: Who united against Attila in Gaul and where was he defeated?
source_text: Franks, Visigoths and the imperial forces united against him and he was defeated at Troyes in a vast dispersed battle in which a multitude of men, variously estimated as between 150,000 and 300,000, were killed.

question: When and in what circumstances did Attila die?
source_text: In 453 Attila died suddenly after a great feast to celebrate his marriage to a young woman, and at his death this plunder confederation of his fell to pieces.

question: Which emperor was suppressed when Constantinople was informed there was no longer an emperor in the west?
source_text: The Vandals chief of the barbarian troops, suppressed a Pannonian who was figuring as emperor under the impressive name of Romulus Augustulus, and informed the Court of Constantinople that there was no longer an emperor in the west.

question: Who was Justinian I married to and what had she been before?
source_text: Justinian I (527-565) was a ruler of very great ambition and energy, and he was married to the Empress Theodora, a woman of quite equal capacity who had begun life as an actress.

question: What new word was the world confronted with by the creed religions?
source_text: These new religions were creed religions. The world was confronted with a new word, Orthodoxy, and with a stern resolve to keep not only acts but speech and private thought within the limits of a set teaching.

question: What did the Roman Empire as an organization fail to do for its citizens?
source_text: did not educate, did not explain itself to its increasing multitudes of citizens, did not invite their co-operation in its decisions.

question: Which cities did Chosroes II take and when did he conquer Egypt?
source_text: At first and until after Heraclius had become Emperor (610) Chosroes II carried all before him. He took Antioch, Damascus and Jerusalem and his armies reached Chalcedon, which is in Asia Minor over against Constantinople. In 619 he conquered Egypt.

question: Where was the message to the Emperor brought in and in which language was it written?
source_text: It had been brought in to the imperial outpost at Bostra south of Damascus; it was in Arabic, an obscure Semitic desert language, and it was read to the Emperor, if it reached him at all, by an interpreter.

question: In which countries did Mongolian peoples establish themselves during the westward drift?
source_text: The Huns of Attila were merely precursors of this advance, which led at last to the establishment of Mongolian peoples in Finland, Esthonia, Hungary and Bulgaria, where their descendants, speaking languages akin to Turkish, survive to this day.

question: Which three things came into use in China during the Suy and Tang period?
source_text: There were great advances in artistic work, in technical skill and in all the amenities of life. Tea was first used, paper manufactured and wood-block printing began.

question: What did Tai-tsung assist Muhammad’s envoys to build in Canton?
source_text: He expressed his interest in their theological ideas and assisted them to build a mosque in Canton, a mosque which survives, it is said, to this day, the oldest mosque in the world.

question: What did Mecca worship at the time of Muhammad and why was it a centre of pilgrimages?
source_text: Mecca was a pagan city at that time worshipping in particular a black stone, the Kaaba, of great repute throughout all Arabia and a centre of pilgrimages;

question: When did Muhammad return to Mecca as its master?
source_text: In 629 Muhammad returned to Mecca as its master, a year after he had sent out these envoys of his to Heraclius, Tai-tsung, Kavadh and all the rulers of the earth.

question: What did Abu Bekr become when Muhammad died and what did he set himself to do?
source_text: And when Muhammad died, Abu Bekr became Caliph (= successor), and with that faith that moves mountains, he set himself simply and sanely to organize the subjugation of the whole world to Allah—with little armies of 3,000 or 4,000 Arabs

question: Which general did the Persians find and at which battle were they broken?
source_text: The Persians had found an able general in Rustam; they had a great host with a force of elephants; and for three days they fought the Arabs at Kadessia (637) and broke at last in headlong rout.

question: When was Spain invaded and where was the Arab advance finally stopped?
source_text: Spain was invaded in 710 and the Pyrenees Mountains were reached in 720. In 732 the Arab advance had reached the centre of France, but here it was stopped for good at the battle of Poitiers and thrust back as far as the Pyrenees again.

question: From whom did the Arab world learn the manufacture of paper?
source_text: It learnt the manufacture of paper—which made printed books possible—from the Chinese.

question: Which numerals replaced the Roman ones, and which words are of Arabic origin?
source_text: The clumsy Roman numerals were ousted by the Arabic figures we use to this day and the zero sign was first employed. The very name algebra is Arabic. So is the word chemistry.

question: Which two chief ends did the Arab alchemists seek in vain?
source_text: One was “the philosopher’s stone”—a means of changing the metallic elements one into another and so getting a control of artificial gold, and the other was the _elixir vitœ_, a stimulant that would revivify age and prolong life indefinitely.

question: What was the lone man prepared to barter under the feudal system?
source_text: Everywhere the lone man felt insecure and was prepared to barter a certain amount of his liberty for help and protection. He sought a stronger man as his lord and protector;

question: Under whose practical rule was the Frankish kingdom when the Moslim crossed the Pyrenees in 720?
source_text: The Moslim when they crossed the Pyrenees in 720 found this Frankish kingdom under the practical rule of Charles Martel, the Mayor of the Palace of a degenerate descendant of Clovis, and experienced the decisive defeat of Poitiers (732) at his hands.

question: What consummated the final rupture between the Latin and the Greek Church, and in which year?
source_text: A dispute about a fine point in the doctrine of the Holy Trinity consummated a long series of dissensions in a final rupture in 1054. The Latin Church and the Greek Church became and remained thereafter distinct and frankly antagonistic.

question: From whom did the Northmen wrest half the kingdom of England, and under whom did they master the whole land?
source_text: The Northmen wrested half the kingdom from his successor Alfred the Great (886), and finally under Canute (1016) made themselves masters of the whole land.

question: Which band of Northmen conquered the north of France and what did it become?
source_text: Under Rolph the Ganger (912) another band of Northmen conquered the north of France, which became Normandy.

question: Which islands did the Northmen sail to and which soil were they the first Europeans to land on?
source_text: They sailed in their galleys even to Iceland and Greenland. They were the first Europeans to land on American soil.

question: Which route did the Magyars take on their raid of 938?
source_text: In 938 they went through Germany into France, crossed the Alps into North Italy, and so came home, burning, robbing and destroying.

question: How and when did the Pope crown Charlemagne?
source_text: The Pope succeeded in crowning his visitor and conqueror by surprise in St. Peter’s on Christmas Day 800 A.D. He produced a crown, put it on the head of Charlemagne and hailed him Cæsar and Augustus.

question: When did the Kingdom of France pass to Hugh Capet and how long did his descendants reign?
source_text: In 987 the Kingdom of France passed out of the possession of the Carlovingian line into the hands of Hugh Capet, whose descendants were still reigning in the eighteenth century.

question: At which battles did Harold King of England win and lose in 1066?
source_text: Harold King of England defeated the former at the battle of Stamford Bridge, and was defeated by the latter at Hastings.

question: Which presents did Haroun-al-Raschid send by his ambassadors?
source_text: It is recorded that Haroun-al-Raschid sent ambassadors from Bagdad—which had now replaced Damascus as the Moslem capital—with a splendid tent, a water clock, an elephant and the keys of the Holy Sepulchre.

question: At which battle was the Byzantine army utterly smashed in 1071?
source_text: In 1071 the Byzantine army was utterly smashed at the battle of Melasgird, and the Turks swept forward until not a trace of Byzantine rule remained in Asia.

question: How did Peter the Hermit carry on his propaganda?
source_text: A man called Peter the Hermit carried on a popular propaganda throughout France and Germany on broadly democratic lines. He went clad in a coarse garment, barefooted on an ass, he carried a huge cross and harangued the crowd in street or market-place or church.

question: Who rallied the forces of Islam in 1169 and when did he recapture Jerusalem?
source_text: In 1169 the forces of Islam were rallied under a Kurdish adventurer named Saladin who had made himself master of Egypt. He preached a Holy War against the Christians, recaptured Jerusalem in 1187, and so provoked the Third Crusade.

question: Against whom did the Latin Church turn in the Fourth Crusade and which city was stormed?
source_text: In the Fourth Crusade (1202-4) the Latin Church turned frankly upon the Greek Empire, and there was not even a pretence of fighting the Turks. It started from Venice and in 1204 it stormed Constantinople.

question: What did Gregory VII oblige the Emperor Henry IV to do at Canossa?
source_text: Gregory VII obliged the Emperor Henry IV to come in penitence to him at Canossa and to await forgiveness for three days and nights in the courtyard of the castle, clad in sackcloth and barefooted to the snow.

question: How much of the land became church property in many European countries?
source_text: Accordingly in many European countries as much as a fourth of the land became church property.

question: Which three countries were placed under an interdict within thirty years at the end of the twelfth century?
source_text: Within thirty years at the end of the twelfth century we find Scotland, France and England in turn under an interdict.

question: Why did Gregory VII make the priests celibates?
source_text: Gregory VII made them celibates; he cut the priests off from too great an intimacy with the laymen in order to bind them more closely to Rome, but indeed he opened a fissure between the church and the commonalty.

question: Which cases were reserved for the clerical courts?
source_text: Cases involving not merely priests but monks, students, crusaders, widows, orphans and the helpless were reserved for the clerical courts, and so were all matters relating to wills, marriages and oaths and all cases of sorcery, heresy and blasphemy.

question: What happened to four followers of St. Francis in 1318?
source_text: his followers, the Franciscans, were persecuted, scourged, imprisoned and dispersed. In 1318 four of them were burnt alive at Marseilles.

question: What organization did Innocent III set up with the assistance of the Dominicans?
source_text: was strongly supported by Innocent III, who with its assistance set up an organization, the Inquisition, for the hunting of heresy and the affliction of free thought.

question: At what age did Innocent III become Pope?
source_text: One of the most vigorous and interesting of the Popes of this great period was Innocent III (1198-1216) who was so fortunate as to become Pope before he was thirty-eight.

question: Whose daughter was Frederick II’s mother, and at what age did he inherit the kingdom of Sicily?
source_text: Frederick was the son of the Emperor Henry VI and his mother was the daughter of Roger I, the Norman King of Sicily. He inherited this kingdom in 1198 when he was a child of four years.

question: What view of religion did Frederick II hold as a result of his double education?
source_text: He got a Moslem view of Christianity as well as a Christian view of Islam, and the unhappy result of this double system of instruction was a view, exceptional in that age of faith, that all religions were impostures.

question: How did Frederick II become King of Jerusalem despite being excommunicated?
